title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: re-extending from every start versus a single coordinated grow-and-shrink sliding window pass.

blocks.text: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. If no such subarray exists, return 0.

blocks.caption: Grow a window until it qualifies, then shrink it from the left to find the smallest valid size

blocks.text: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if no such subarray exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Packing the Smallest Bag That Meets a Weight Requirement
blocks.text: Like adding items to a bag one at a time until its total weight is finally enough, then checking whether removing items from the front still keeps it heavy enough, to find the smallest possible qualifying bag.

blocks.caption: Add items until the bag is heavy enough, then trim from the front while it still qualifies

blocks.text: The total sum of the entire array is only 8, which never reaches the target of 11, so no qualifying subarray exists at all, and the answer is 0.
Before checking every possible subarray directly, notice that every value in nums is positive, a detail that unlocks a much faster approach.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every element is positive, extending a subarray to the right can only ever increase its sum, and shrinking it from the left can only ever decrease its sum. Sums move in a single, predictable direction as the window changes.

Observation 2: This means once a window's sum reaches at least target, shrinking it from the left is always safe to attempt, since you can immediately tell whether it still qualifies.

Observation 3: Grow a window from the right, one element at a time. The moment its sum reaches target, shrink from the left as much as possible while it still qualifies, recording the shortest such window found.

Observation 4: Since each position is added to the window exactly once and removed at most once, the entire process runs in a single pass, touching each element a constant number of times overall.

Whenever a problem needs the shortest (or longest) subarray satisfying a sum-based condition, and every value is positive, a variable-size sliding window that grows and shrinks in one coordinated pass is almost always the fastest approach.
This "grow until valid, then shrink while still valid" strategy is the standard shape of every variable-size sliding window problem.
For every possible starting position, extend the subarray to the right until its sum reaches target, then record its length.

items: For every possible starting position, extend the subarray one element at a time, maintaining a running total.

The moment the running total reaches target, record the current length and stop extending from this particular start, since extending further would only produce a longer, not shorter, subarray from this start.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop breaks immediately once a qualifying subarray is found for the current start, since any longer subarray from that same start can never be shorter, and thus never beats the current candidate.
A running total is maintained incrementally within each start's inner loop, rather than resumming from scratch at every single end position.
min_len starts at infinity so that any real qualifying length found will correctly replace it, and stays at infinity (mapped to 0) only if truly nothing qualifies.

blocks.text: Every possible starting position is checked directly, extending until the target is reached, so the correct minimum length is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since each of the n starting positions can extend up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: restarting the running total from scratch at every new starting position ignores that the array's positivity guarantees a much more efficient, coordinated single-pass approach.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force treats every starting position independently, discarding useful information between them. But because every value is positive, a single running window can be grown and shrunk together in one coordinated pass: grow the window from the right until its sum reaches target, then greedily shrink it from the left for as long as it keeps qualifying, recording the shortest length seen at each point. Since the left pointer only ever moves forward and never resets, the total amount of work across the entire pass stays linear.

Maintain a window with a left and right boundary. Grow the window by advancing right and adding to a running sum. Whenever the running sum reaches target, repeatedly shrink from the left (removing from the running sum and advancing left) while the window still qualifies, recording the shortest qualifying length seen.
Grow the window from the right, and greedily shrink it from the left whenever it still qualifies.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since left and right each advance forward at most n times total across the whole pass.
Space: O(1) extra.

Because every value in nums is positive, the running sum increases monotonically whenever right advances and decreases monotonically whenever left advances. This monotonic behavior guarantees that once a window qualifies (sum at least target), shrinking it from the left is always a safe, well-defined operation: the sum only decreases, and the process of shrinking naturally finds the smallest qualifying window ending at the current right position, before the window is grown further.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Running sum is still below target","Keep growing the window by advancing right"],["Running sum reaches or exceeds target","Record the current length, then shrink from the left while the window still qualifies, recording each shorter qualifying length along the way"]]}

items: The right pointer drives a single outer loop, always advancing forward and never resetting.

The inner while loop shrinks the window from the left for as long as it still qualifies, updating the best length at every valid shrink, which is what correctly finds the minimum length ending at the current right position.
Because left only ever moves forward and never backward, the total number of shrink operations across the entire run is bounded by n, keeping the overall algorithm linear.

blocks.text: When every value in an array is positive and a problem asks for the shortest (or longest) subarray meeting a sum-based condition, a variable-size sliding window that grows and shrinks together in one pass is almost always the right tool.

items: Using a fixed-size window instead of a variable-size one, when the problem is actually asking for the best possible LENGTH, not a specific fixed length.
Forgetting that positivity is what makes shrinking safe; this exact technique would not directly work if nums could contain negative numbers, since the sum would no longer change monotonically.
Not correctly mapping "no qualifying window found" (an initial sentinel value like infinity) back to the required output of 0.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["No subarray ever reaches target (total sum of nums is too small)","Correctly returns 0, since the sentinel minimum length is never updated"],["A single element already meets or exceeds target","Correctly returns 1, the shortest possible non-empty subarray length"]]}

items: Explicitly point out that the array's positivity is what justifies safely shrinking the window, since this is the key insight an interviewer is listening for.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the shortest (or longest) subarray meeting a sum condition, with all positive values" points toward a variable-size sliding window: grow from the right, shrink from the left whenever the window still qualifies.

items: How would this change if nums could contain negative numbers? The sliding window approach would break, since shrinking would no longer reliably decrease the sum; a prefix-sum-based approach (potentially with a monotonic deque) would be needed instead.

How would you find the total COUNT of qualifying subarrays, rather than just the shortest one? A similar sliding window could count how many subarrays ending at each right position qualify, summing these counts.

What if you needed the LONGEST subarray with sum at MOST some target, instead of the shortest with sum at LEAST some target? The same sliding window shape applies, just with the growth and shrink conditions flipped.

The same "grow until valid, shrink while still valid" shape appears throughout this category, such as in Longest Repeating Character Replacement and Max Consecutive Ones III, just with different validity conditions.
Contrasts with fixed-size sliding window problems (like Maximum Average Subarray I), where the window size itself never changes.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (variable-size sliding window): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Variable-size sliding window, growing from the right and greedily shrinking from the left once valid
Core Idea: Since all values are positive, the window's sum changes monotonically, making it safe to shrink from the left as soon as the window qualifies
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Positivity guarantees the sum only ever increases when growing and only ever decreases when shrinking, which is what makes a coordinated single-pass window valid
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Grow until it is heavy enough, then trim from the front while it still is
